'''Bryan Campbell Clarke''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS}}<ref name=rsbm>{{Cite journal | last1 = Clarke | first1 = Bryan Campbell | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.1995.0010  | doi-access = free| title = Edmund Brisco Ford. 23 April 1901 – 2 January 1988 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 41 | pages = 146–168| year = 1995 |publisher=[[Royal Society]]|location=London|jstor=770139| s2cid = 72984345 }}</ref> (24 June 1932&nbsp;– 27 February 2014) was a British Professor of [[genetics]], latterly [[emeritus]] at the [[University of Nottingham]]. Clarke is particularly noted for his work on [[apostatic selection]] (which is a term he coined in 1962) and other forms of frequency-dependent selection, and work on [[polymorphism (biology)|polymorphism]] in snails, much of it done during the 1960s. Later, he studied [[molecular evolution]]. He made the case for [[natural selection]] as an important factor in the maintenance of molecular variation, and in driving evolutionary changes in molecules through time. In doing so, he questioned the over-riding importance of random [[genetic drift]] advocated by King, Jukes, and Kimura. With Professor James J Murray Jnr (University of Virginia), he carried out an extensive series of studies on speciation in land snails of the genus ''[[Partula (gastropod)|Partula]]'' inhabiting the volcanic islands of the Eastern Pacific. These studies helped illuminate the genetic changes that take place during the origin of species.

==Education==
Clarke was educated at [[Magdalen College, Oxford]], receiving a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1956<ref name="RoySoc"/> followed by a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] degree in 1961 from the [[University of Oxford]] for research investigating factors affecting shell colour [[Polymorphism (biology)|polymorphism]] in the land snails (''[[Cepaea]]'').<ref name=clarkedphil>{{cite thesis|degree=DPhil|first=Bryan Campbell|last=Clarke|title=Some factors affecting shell colour polymorphism in Cepaea|publisher=University of Oxford|year=1961|url=http://solo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/OXVU1:LSCOP_OX:oxfaleph020439045|website=bodleian.ox.ac.uk|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.483984}}|oclc=556424167|archive-date=13 December 2019|access-date=25 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191213184629/http://solo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/OXVU1:LSCOP_OX:oxfaleph020439045|url-status=dead}} {{free access}}</ref>

==Career and research==
Clarke was appointed a [[Lecturer]] at the [[University of Edinburgh]] in 1959<ref name = "RoySoc"/> and was promoted to [[Reader (academic rank)|Reader]] by the time he left in 1971. In 1971 he became Foundation Professor at the new Department of Genetics at the [[University of Nottingham]] becoming Emeritus Professor in 1997. During this period he spent two spells (1971–76, 1981–93) as Head of Department.

Clarke mentored many scientists in evolutionary genetics, supervising more than thirty research students, many of which went gone on to successful research careers themselves such as [[Steve Jones (biologist)|Steve Jones]].<ref name=jonesphd>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|first=John Stephen |last=Jones|title=Studies on the Ecological Genetics of ''Cepaea''|publisher=University of Edinburgh|year=1971|url=https://www.era.lib.ed.ac.uk/handle/1842/15121|website=lib.ed.ac.uk|hdl=1842/15121|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.653149}}|oclc=606118378}} {{free access}}</ref> He was a co-founder of the [[Population Genetics]] Group ("PopGroup") a scientific meeting for evolutionary and population genetics held annually in the UK since the 1960s.<ref>{{cite web|title=Previous Meetings|url=http://populationgeneticsgroup.org.uk/previous-meetings/|website=Population Genetics Group|accessdate=17 September 2016|archive-date=30 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180930082917/http://populationgeneticsgroup.org.uk/previous-meetings/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Clarke was co-founder (with his wife [[Ann Clarke (immunologist)|Ann]] and Dame [[Anne McLaren]]) and trustee of the [[Frozen Ark]] project, launched in 2004 to preserve the DNA and living cells of endangered species worldwide.<ref name="frozenark">{{cite web |title=People |url=https://www.frozenark.org/people/ |publisher=The Frozen Ark |accessdate=9 February 2020 |archive-date=12 November 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191112171623/https://www.frozenark.org/people/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=obit-telegraph />

Clarke acted as managing editor of the scientific journal ''[[Heredity (journal)|Heredity]]'' from 1978 to 1985.<ref name=obit-telegraph>{{cite web|url= https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/10678384/Professor-Bryan-Clarke-obituary.html| title = Professor Bryan Clarke - obituary
| date = 5 March 2014
|publisher = The Telegraph|accessdate= 10 March 2014}}</ref>

===Awards and achievements===
Clarke was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1982.<ref name="RoySoc">{{Cite journal |last=Brookfield |first=John |title=Bryan Campbell Clarke. 24 June 1932 — 27 February 2014 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |year=2023 |volume=74|pages=109–121 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.2022.0042 |s2cid=164222926 |doi-access=free }}</ref> In 2003 he was both awarded the [[Linnean Medal]] for Zoology and elected a Foreign member of the [[American Philosophical Society]]. In 2004 he was elected a Foreign Honorary Member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]. He received one of the thirteen [[Darwin-Wallace Medal]]s awarded by the [[Linnean Society of London]] in 2008; at that time the award was made only every 50 years.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Darwin-Wallace medal|url=https://www.linnean.org/the-society/medals-awards-prizes-grants/the-darwin-wallace-medal|website=The Linnean Society of London|accessdate=19 December 2016}}</ref> He was awarded the [[Darwin Medal]] of the Royal Society in 2010 'for his original and influential contributions to our understanding of the genetic basis of evolution'.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://royalsociety.org/Darwin-Medal/| title = The Darwin Medal (1890)|publisher = The Royal Society|accessdate= 13 August 2010}}</ref>

In 1959 he published ''Berber Village'', an account of an Oxford University expedition to the High Atlas mountains of Morocco.<ref>''Berber Village. The Story of the Oxford University Expedition to the High Atlas Mountains of Morocco.'' Longmans, Travel Book Club.</ref>
